Using 3.0 inverse femtobarns of LHCb data from the 2016 LHC run, the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay rate was studied to determine the $B^0_s$ meson's effective lifetime. The analysis yielded an effective lifetime of 1.44 inverse picoseconds with an uncertainty of 0.06 inverse picoseconds. This result was compared to theoretical predictions and previous measurements from the Belle and Belle II collaborations.

This study examines the numerical solution to a control problem involving a stochastic partial differential equation, where the control is subject to constraints and the equation's coefficients are influenced by random fluctuations. The research derives a discrete approximation for the optimal control and solution, establishing a convergence rate of order one in time and space. Additionally, the paper presents a convergent numerical scheme with explicit error bounds.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has detected a significant anisotropy in the distribution of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays with energies exceeding 4 EeV. This observation is characterized by a dipole anisotropy that varies seasonally, with an amplitude of 10.0% and a direction that shifts by 63 degrees over the course of a year. The anisotropy's axis is inclined at an angle of 24 degrees from the celestial equator, and its orientation changes by 63 degrees over the course of a year. The data also reveals a quadrupole anisotropy that fluctuates between 2% and 10% throughout the year. The direction of the observed anisotropy is consistent with the direction of the Perseus galaxy cluster, located 240 Mpc away. The anisotropy's amplitude and direction are in agreement with theoretical predictions based on the LHAASO observation of a 100 PeV gamma-ray source in the direction of the Perseus galaxy cluster.

This research paper proves that all infinite-dimensional, finitely generated Zinbiel algebras are necessarily nilpotent, building on the original definition of these algebras introduced by A. A. Beidar, M. L. Rodman, and R. H. Sharp in 1991.

The initial geometry of the quark-gluon plasma created in heavy ion collisions is influenced by fluctuations in the impact parameter, which can be analyzed through the angle and magnitude of the average elliptic flow. This study examines the elliptic flow angle and magnitude fluctuations in lead-lead collisions at a top energy of 5.02 TeV, utilizing the angle and magnitude of the initial spatial anisotropy as proxies for the initial geometry. The findings reveal that the distribution of the elliptic flow angle is consistent with a Gaussian shape, with a width of 0.11 radians, and the magnitude of the initial spatial anisotropy is found to be smaller than anticipated from a simple geometric model.

This research focuses on resolving inconsistencies in tabular data that contain null values and adhere to specific functional relationships. We define a new concept called a repair, which represents a valid table derived from an inconsistent one by modifying only the non-null data points. We then explore the challenge of identifying the repair that minimizes the number of altered data points, specifically in the context of first-order functional dependencies. We demonstrate that this problem is computationally complex, but also provide an efficient solution for a specific subset of dependencies. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of finding the best possible set of dependencies that can explain the data, and show that this task is also computationally complex. We then present an algorithm that can solve this problem for a specific subset of dependencies, and also provide an alternative approach that involves relaxing the dependencies.

We introduce a novel class of models called time-varying Poisson autoregressive (TV-POIR) models, which are designed to analyze count data that exhibit dynamic dependencies over time. These models are capable of capturing complex relationships between variables and can be used to forecast future values and identify key drivers of change. We develop a Bayesian estimation method for TV-POIR models and apply them to a dataset of monthly US manufacturing production data. Our findings reveal that certain manufacturing sectors have a significant impact on overall production levels, and that the strength of these relationships fluctuates over time.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel approach for representing 3D objects in a way that is invariant to pose and enables efficient retrieval and manipulation. This method encodes objects using a neural network that outputs a descriptor at each point in space, and leverages the fact that descriptor fields are smooth to reduce the number of parameters needed. We show that this approach can be used for both object retrieval and grasping tasks, and outperforms existing methods in terms of performance and sample efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/toni0000/ndf.

The complex zeros of the partition function in the complex plane are a key aspect of statistical mechanics, and their behavior is classified into universality classes. A significant feature of these classes is the Yang-Lee edge singularity, which marks the point closest to the real axis. In this study, we have determined the position of the Yang-Lee edge for the classic O(N) universality classes, specifically for N = 0, 1, 2, and 3, and found that their edge locations are 0.47466(10), 0.47466(10), 0.47466(10), and 0.47466(10) times the lattice spacing. These findings are consistent with previous research and have been derived using the renormalization group method, which involves a new approach to the epsilon expansion that can be applied to other classic universality classes.

We introduce a novel concept of operator convexity for analytic functions, which encompasses the standard definition of convexity for functions of real variables. This new notion is applied to demonstrate the local convexity of the TAP free energy function around its stationary points. Furthermore, we establish a variant of the Sudakov-Fernique comparison principle that holds for the 2-Wasserstein metric, which is used to prove the local convexity of the TAP free energy.

The use of photometry from stars to measure atmospheric aerosols has been a subject of interest for astronomers and atmospheric scientists for several decades. This technique relies on the principle that aerosols in the atmosphere can scatter and absorb light from stars, causing variations in the brightness of the stars as observed from the ground. In this paper, we provide an overview of the fundamental principles behind this technique, discuss the types of measurements that can be made using this technique, and highlight some of the key applications of this technique in studying the Earth's atmosphere. We also review the main challenges and limitations of this technique, and outline the main areas of research that are needed to overcome these challenges.

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the pose of objects in 3D space using point clouds. Our method, called DeepHMap++, combines two techniques: projection grouping and correspondence learning. This combination allows for more accurate pose estimation by leveraging the strengths of both methods. Our approach is designed to work with objects that have complex shapes and can handle point clouds with missing data. To train our model, we created a new dataset called ShapeNetPart, which contains over 100,000 labeled parts from various objects. Our experiments show that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in estimating the pose of objects with complex shapes and partial point clouds.

High-dimensional covariance estimation is a critical task in various fields, and the Graphical Lasso method is a widely used approach for this purpose. The Graphical Lasso method produces a sparse inverse covariance matrix, which can be used to create a graph that represents the conditional independence relationships between variables. In this paper, we present a Python package called GGLasso, which is designed to perform General Graphical Lasso computation. The GGLasso package is capable of handling both symmetric and non-symmetric inverse covariance matrices, and it can be used to generate various types of graphs, including undirected, directed, and mixed graphs. The package is built on top of the popular Python package called CVXPY, which is used for convex optimization. The GGLasso package is also accompanied by a set of examples and documentation that can be found on GitHub.

A key challenge in computational chemistry and molecular biology is accurately predicting the behavior of complex molecules, which is hindered by the vast number of possible molecular configurations. To address this issue, researchers have developed various methods to efficiently sample the possible configurations of molecules, including molecular dynamics simulations. However, these methods can be computationally expensive, particularly when dealing with large molecules. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that combines the Langevin dynamics simulation method with a new, efficient integrator, which allows for the accurate and efficient sampling of molecular configurations, even when dealing with large molecules. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations of small molecules and a large protein, showing that our method can significantly reduce the computational cost of sampling molecular configurations.

The concept of centrality in networks is a fundamental aspect that has been extensively studied, particularly in the context of single-layer networks. However, many real-world networks are composed of multiple interconnected layers, and the centrality of a node in these multilayer networks is influenced by its connections across different layers. This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing multilayer networks, where the importance of a node can vary across different layers, and develops a new measure of eigenvector centrality based on this framework. The proposed centrality measure is mathematically equivalent to the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix that represents the multilayer network, and the paper derives explicit expressions for the eigenvector centrality of a node in terms of the connections within its own layer and other layers. The paper also provides a numerical example to illustrate the proposed framework and centrality measure.

In this paper, we derive the Dirac equation within the framework of Riemann-Cartan spacetime, taking into account the torsion field. We begin by formulating the Dirac action in R-Minkowski spacetime and then apply the principle of least action to obtain the Dirac equation. We also explore the implications of the torsion field on the Dirac equation and discuss its physical significance.

When a sphere rapidly enters water, a thin layer of air gets trapped beneath it, forming an air cavity. This cavity's stability is crucial for underwater applications, as it can either remain intact or break, releasing a jet of water. The conditions that determine whether the cavity remains sealed or breaks are complex and depend on various factors. This study focuses on the conditions that lead to cavity seal breakage, specifically examining the relationship between the sphere's entry speed and the size of the cavity. By analyzing cavity dynamics, we found that the cavity seal breakage is influenced by the size of the cavity and the sphere's entry speed. The study also presents a new dimensionless parameter that can be used to predict the conditions that lead to cavity seal breakage. This parameter is based on the cavity's size and the sphere's entry speed, and it provides a useful tool for understanding the conditions that lead to cavity seal breakage.

We investigate the low-energy effective theories of Type IIB string theory incorporating D-branes and orientifold planes, focusing on configurations that allow for a broad range of moduli and non-perturbative contributions to the superpotential. By analyzing these setups, we demonstrate that certain configurations can lead to spontaneous breaking of global symmetries and the emergence of generalized theta-terms in the effective theory. Specifically, we find that the vacuum expectation values of non-perturbatively generated fields can result in the spontaneous breaking of the shift symmetry of the axion, thereby inducing a generalized theta-term in the effective theory. Furthermore, we show that the number of non-perturbatively generated fields can be made arbitrarily large, leading to a variety of possible symmetry-breaking patterns and theta-term contributions.

Cubanite, a common sulfide mineral, is known for its distinctive copper luster and is frequently mistaken for chalcopyrite. Although these two minerals share a similar chemical composition, cubanite is a semiconducting material, whereas chalcopyrite is a metal. This difference in conductivity is attributed to the unique crystal structure of cubanite, which is characterized by a distorted face-centered cubic lattice. The structure of cubanite is further complicated by the presence of two distinct iron sites, which exhibit different local environments. To investigate the electronic properties of cubanite, we conducted a series of first-principles calculations, which revealed that the Fe 3d states in the material are highly localized and exhibit orbital selectivity. Specifically, the Fe 3d states in the (111) plane are found to be more localized than those in the (100) plane, which is attributed to the unique local environment of the iron sites. The calculations also revealed that the material exhibits a Mott-like state, which is characterized by a large energy gap and a high degree of electron localization. The unique electronic properties of cubanite are further influenced by the presence of a large spin-orbit coupling, which is found to be responsible for the formation of a topological surface state in the material. The findings of this study provide new insights into the electronic properties of cubanite and may have implications for the development of novel semiconducting materials.

We observed exceptionally large Rabi oscillations in a semiconductor quantum dot, specifically in a dark exciton system, where the Rabi frequency was found to be 1.5 GHz, which is 10 times greater than what is typically expected. This phenomenon was discovered in a GaAs quantum dot, where the electron and hole spins are decoupled due to their weak interaction with the external magnetic field. The large Rabi frequency was found to be directly proportional to the strength of the applied electric field, which was manipulated by adjusting the voltage on a nearby gate electrode. This relationship was found to hold true for both dark and bright exciton systems, and the findings were confirmed through numerical simulations. The ability to control the Rabi frequency through the application of an external electric field opens up new possibilities for manipulating quantum states in semiconductor quantum dots.

The electronic structure of two-dimensional materials is significantly influenced by non-symmorphic symmetries, which can lead to the formation of protected Dirac points. However, the limited number of wallpaper groups with non-symmorphic symmetries has hindered the discovery of novel materials with these properties. In this study, we introduce a new non-symmorphic wallpaper group, denoted as p2mg, and investigate its potential to host protected Dirac points in two-dimensional materials. We demonstrate that the p2mg group can be realized in various compound structures, including honeycomb lattices, Kagome lattices, and triangular lattices. By employing first-principles calculations, we identify specific materials with the p2mg group that exhibit massless Dirac fermions, including the compounds Li2PdTe2, Li2PdSe2, and Li2PdS2. Furthermore, we explore the tunability of these materials by introducing a second type of atom, which can be used to manipulate the position of the Dirac points. This study highlights the potential of non-symmorphic symmetries in the discovery of novel materials with unique electronic properties.

Quantum light fields, particularly non-classical states, are essential for advancing quantum technologies. A notable non-classical state is the single-photon catalyzed coherent state (SPCCS), which is of significant interest due to its potential applications in quantum communication and computation. This research introduces a novel method for generating the single-photon catalyzed coherent state using quantum-optical catalysis. The proposed method involves a single-photon input field interacting with a single-mode cavity containing a single atom, which is driven by a classical field. The interaction is carefully controlled to ensure that the single-photon input field is amplified, resulting in the generation of the single-photon catalyzed coherent state within the cavity. The research also investigates the impact of various parameters on the generated state and demonstrates the potential for generating the single-photon catalyzed coherent state using this method.

In the context of General Relativity, the use of complex null tetrads is a common approach, which is particularly well-suited for the Newman-Penrose formalism. This method involves expressing tensor equations using complex scalar components, and is especially effective for analyzing systems of partial differential equations. In this paper, we provide a detailed derivation of the Weyl curvature tensor in terms of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, and we also obtain the five Newman-Penrose equations for the Weyl tensor.

This paper presents a novel approach to identifying polymers from molecular formulas, combining linear regression and integer programming. The proposed method, called PolymersInference, takes a molecular formula as input and determines the smallest repeating unit that constitutes the polymer. The process involves two main steps: first, linear regression is used to find a potential repeating unit that matches the input formula, and second, integer programming is employed to verify if the repeating unit can be scaled to match the input formula exactly. The PolymersInference method was tested on a dataset of 1000 molecules, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately inferring polymers. The code for this method is available on GitHub.

Accurate segmentation of esophageal tumors in CT images is a critical step in
developing effective treatment plans for cancer patients. However, this task is
challenging due to the varying shapes and sizes of tumors, as well as the presence
of noise and artifacts in CT images. In this study, we introduce a novel deep
learning model called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet) to address this
problem. Our model combines several advanced techniques, including dilated
convolutions, dense connections, and self-attention mechanisms, to improve the
accuracy of tumor segmentation. We evaluated our model on two public datasets,
the Kvasir dataset and the TUH dataset, and found that it outperforms existing
state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy. Our results indicate
that the DDAUnet model is a promising approach for segmenting esophageal tumors in
CT images and could have significant implications for improving cancer diagnosis
and treatment.

Multilingualism is a common feature of many societies, and multilingual communication is a daily occurrence. However, the study of multilingual communication has been hindered by the lack of suitable datasets and the complexity of developing models that can handle multiple languages. In this paper, we discuss the challenges and considerations of code-switching NLP, which is a related but distinct phenomenon from multilingualism. We also highlight the importance of considering sociolinguistic factors in NLP research and discuss the potential benefits of code-switching NLP research. In doing so, we aim to provide a foundation for future work in this area and encourage the development of models that can accurately reflect the diversity of multilingual societies.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to evaluate automatic image description systems. However, this method has limitations due to potential inaccuracies in the reference descriptions. This study investigates the reliability of human reference descriptions by analyzing their consistency and similarity to automatically generated descriptions. The findings reveal that while human reference descriptions are generally consistent, they also contain errors. Furthermore, the study found that the quality of automatic descriptions can be improved by filtering out unreliable reference descriptions. The study also presents a new dataset, consisting of 10,000 images with multiple descriptions from different sources, to facilitate the evaluation of automatic image description systems.

Tantalum oxide (Ta$_2$O$_5$) is a technologically important material with a complex crystal structure, making it difficult to study. To address this challenge, researchers have used first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the material's properties and potential applications. The study found that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a unique crystal structure with a large band gap, and that its structure can be modified by applying pressure or changing its composition. The study also identified several potential applications for Ta$_2$O$_5$, including in optical coatings and solid-state electronics. Overall, the research provides valuable insights into the material's properties and potential uses, and may help to advance the development of new technologies based on tantalum oxide.

A significant aspect of Reddit's growth in the United States is the "Big Geographic Sort," which has led to a substantial increase in the platform's reach across different regions. This phenomenon has been shown to facilitate the spread of false information, as demonstrated in a study that examined the circulation of a fabricated news story about the 2016 U.S. presidential election on Reddit. The research found that users who typically engage with local news were more likely to share the misinformation, while those who usually consume national news were less likely to do so. This finding is consistent with existing theories on the role of geographic distance in the spread of false information. The research also highlights the importance of considering the diverse user base of Reddit and the potential for the platform to be used to spread false information across different regions.

The effectiveness of robots that learn from human demonstrations depends heavily on the quality of the data they are trained on. While robots can learn from videos or text-based instructions, learning from the spoken guidance of human teachers has proven to be a more natural and efficient method. However, the spoken instructions given by humans are often filled with unnecessary filler words and variations in language that can hinder the learning process. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the spoken instructions given by humans during manipulation tasks, revealing that the language used is concise and purposeful, with little to no filler words. The findings suggest that the spoken instructions given by humans are highly informative and can be used to improve the learning process for robots.

We investigate the time evolution of quantum field theory complexity, specifically in the context of CFTs in one spatial dimension. By employing the classical/semiclassical approximation, we establish a connection between the dynamics of complexity and the Euler-Arnold equations, which govern the behavior of a free boson. This connection allows us to derive the time evolution of the expectation value of the density of the Hamiltonian for a free boson in its ground state. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the dynamics of complexity and the dynamics of the vacuum in the presence of a conformal field redefinition.

Conversational agents are increasingly used in various applications, and their effectiveness is often evaluated through subjective user feedback. However, this type of feedback can be influenced by individual biases and may not accurately reflect the agent's performance. To address this issue, we have developed an automated testing framework that enables the creation of reproducible and objective tests for conversational agents. This framework allows for the development of tests that can be run multiple times, facilitating the comparison of different agent implementations. We have demonstrated the utility of this framework by creating a test suite for a chatbot designed to assist users in navigating the University of Edinburgh's website.

In today's data-driven world, recommendation systems are essential for navigating vast amounts of information. However, these systems face significant challenges due to their reliance on user-provided data, which is often incomplete and sparse. This issue is compounded in multi-domain collaborative recommendation, where data sparsity is exacerbated across multiple domains. To address this problem, we propose a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation via Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (MSD-CRAPL). This approach leverages the interconnected nature of different domains to facilitate knowledge transfer and enhance recommendation accuracy. Specifically, we introduce a mechanism for identifying and transferring relevant information across domains, as well as a method for capturing the complex relationships between users and aspects within each domain. Our approach is designed to handle the inherent complexity of multi-domain data, which is characterized by its high dimensionality and non-linear relationships. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing methods in terms of recommendation accuracy.

Convex optimization problems can be solved efficiently using second-order cone programming and semidefinite programming, which are based on conic formulations. These formulations are natural and intuitive, and they can be converted into standard forms using tools like Convex.jl. However, this conversion process can be computationally expensive and may result in a loss of sparsity in the problem's structure. In this paper, we propose a new approach that converts conic formulations into standard form while preserving their original structure and with a low computational cost. Our method is demonstrated using a portfolio optimization problem with copula risk measures, and our results show that our conversion process is faster and more accurate than the existing approach.

The rapid advancement of MRI technology has led to a significant increase in the number of acquired images, but this has also resulted in a growing prevalence of corrupted images due to technical issues and human error. These corrupted images can negatively impact the performance of deep learning models, which are increasingly used in medical imaging. To address this issue, we propose a novel quality control framework that leverages deep learning to automatically detect corrupted images. Our approach is based on a multi-factorial generalization problem, which involves training a model to recognize the relationship between various quality control factors and the resulting image quality. Our framework is evaluated on two large-scale datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting corrupted images.

The increasing prevalence of private electric vehicles (PEVs) has significantly influenced the reliability of power distribution systems, especially during extreme weather events. This study investigates the impact of PEVs on system resilience by considering the operational decisions made by individual owners. A novel multi-agent optimization framework is developed to model these decisions, taking into account the trade-off between maintaining power and preserving battery charge. The framework is applied to a case study of a distribution system affected by a hurricane, revealing that PEVs can both hinder and enhance system resilience depending on the severity of the event and the timing of charging. The study also highlights the potential for PEVs to support system resilience through battery-to-grid technology, and the need for further research to fully understand and leverage this capability.

This paper presents a novel approach to multi-agent recurrent rendezvous, where agents meet repeatedly at a specific location. Unlike previous studies, our method incorporates agents with memory and motivation, enabling them to learn and adapt to changing environments. Our approach utilizes a recurrent network to remember past experiences and a drive-based motivation system to guide agents towards their goal. Our results demonstrate that this approach enables agents to successfully meet at a designated location, even in dynamic environments.

By applying the concept of information entropy to the distribution of hadrons, we have developed a statistical model that can be used to predict the abundance of various types of hadrons. Our model is based on the assumption that the distribution of hadrons is governed by the principle of maximum information entropy, which states that the most likely distribution is the one that maximizes the amount of information contained in the data. Our model is shown to be in good agreement with experimental data from particle colliders, and it can be used to predict the abundance of various types of hadrons, including protons, neutrons, pions, and kaons. Our model also provides a new way of understanding the composition of ordinary matter, and it can be used to predict the abundance of various types of matter in different astrophysical environments, including stars, planets, and galaxies.

This paper proves a generalized version of the B-type Coxeter group basis theorem, which states that the set of signed permutations $\sigma$ satisfying specific conditions—where the number of descents is at most $k$, the number of signed descents is at most $l$, and the sum of the positions of the signed descents is at most $m$—forms a basis for the $k$-th cohomology of the configuration space of $n$ points in the plane.

The distribution of dark matter on large scales is being studied through gravitational lensing, specifically weak lensing, which affects the brightness of distant supernovae. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers have utilized the Pantheon sample of Type Ia supernovae, which includes 1038 well-characterized events. By analyzing the Pantheon sample, the team has been able to estimate the relationship between the brightness of supernovae and the mass of foreground galaxy clusters, which is essential for understanding weak lensing. They have also developed a method to correct for biases in the data caused by the selection process used to identify supernovae. Using this method, the researchers have been able to estimate the average brightness of supernovae behind galaxy clusters, which is a key parameter for understanding weak lensing. T centres in silicon are a type of point defect that exhibit photoluminescence in the visible spectrum and are of interest for quantum information processing. This study investigates the T centre in silicon photonic material, specifically focusing on the impact of the buried oxide layer on their optical properties. By utilizing a scanning confocal microscope, researchers have been able to map the spatial distribution of T centres in silicon-on-insulator samples. The study reveals that T centres are more prevalent in the channel region of the samples, and their spatial distribution is influenced by the thickness of the buried oxide layer. The study also provides a detailed analysis of the T centre's spin states and their coherence times, which are found to be comparable to those observed in bulk silicon. The findings of this study have implications for the development of T centre-based quantum information processing in silicon photonic material.

Object detection in images is a challenging task that requires a deep understanding of the context. While many deep learning-based detectors excel at identifying objects, they often struggle with context, which is crucial for accurately locating objects in complex scenes. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to evaluate the context of objects detected by deep learning models. Our method involves creating a context map that represents the spatial distribution of objects in an image, and we use this map to identify areas of high context relevance. We then apply this context information to improve the performance of object detectors by re-weighting the scores of objects in high-context areas. Our proposed approach is evaluated on the COCO dataset and shows significant improvements in object detection performance.

This study investigates a nonhomogeneous Kirchhoff-type elliptic system in two dimensions, featuring the singular Trudinger-Moser growth and a coefficient that diverges at the origin. By applying variational methods and critical point theory, we establish the existence of multiple solutions, including a pair of sign-definite solutions and a solution that changes sign.

This paper derives concentration inequalities for a class of binary random variables that exhibit negative dependence, specifically those that are negatively associated and pairwise negatively dependent. By applying these results to the random coloring of graphs, we obtain an upper bound on the probability that the number of monochromatic edges exceeds a certain threshold.

A symplectic transformation is a linear mapping that preserves the structure of a phase space, specifically the Poisson brackets of canonical coordinates. These transformations are fundamental in Hamiltonian mechanics, as they maintain the invariance of Hamilton's equations under a change of coordinates. This paper provides an elementary proof of Darboux's theorem, which states that any Hamiltonian system can be locally transformed into a canonical system. Additionally, it offers a straightforward proof of the fact that the set of symplectic transformations forms a group, known as the symplectic group.

Incompatible kidney transplants are often rejected by the recipient's immune system, but advancements in medicine have made them a viable option. This study focuses on determining the optimal conditions under which incompatible kidney transplants should be accepted. It considers various factors, including the quality of the kidney, the risk of rejection, and the possibility of administering a life-saving drug. The research finds that incompatible kidney transplants should be accepted if the kidney is of high quality and the risk of rejection is low. It also suggests that administering a life-saving drug should be reserved for cases where the risk of rejection is high. The study provides a mathematical framework for decision-making in incompatible kidney transplants and offers insights into the optimal conditions under which these transplants should be accepted.

The integration of natural language processing (NLP) into financial analysis has gained significant attention in recent years. This study investigates the effectiveness of NLP techniques, specifically word embeddings, in capturing the nuances of financial news, particularly in the context of stock market trading. To do this, we examine the Loughran-McDonald (LM) financial sentiment dictionary, a widely used resource for sentiment analysis. Our findings reveal that the LM dictionary is not fully reflected in word embeddings, as evidenced by the low correlation between the dictionary's polarity scores and the embeddings' cosine similarities. Furthermore, we found that the dictionary's polarity scores are not consistent across different embedding models, and that the dictionary's structure is not well-represented in the embedding space. These results suggest that the LM dictionary may not be a reliable tool for sentiment analysis, and that alternative approaches may be needed to accurately capture the nuances of financial news.

A novel numerical approach is proposed to solve the Stefan problem, which involves a moving boundary between solid and liquid phases. This method combines level-set and embedded boundary techniques to track the interface and calculate temperature and velocity fields. By utilizing an embedded boundary technique, the domain is divided into a fine mesh for the liquid phase and a coarser mesh for the solid phase, allowing for more efficient computation. The method also employs a fictitious domain technique to solve the velocity and temperature equations in the liquid phase. Numerical results demonstrate the method's accuracy and efficiency, particularly in handling complex geometries and large temperature differences.

In multiplayer games, a player's strategy is influenced by their beliefs about other players' actions. A key aspect of this is the assumption that players hold rational views about each other. This paper focuses on a specific type of rationality, where players believe other players' actions are influenced by their own private information. This concept is formalized using a graphical model, which represents the relationships between players and their private information. This model is used to define a new type of equilibrium, called the Graphical Rationalizable Equilibrium (GRE), which is based on the assumption that players' beliefs are influenced by their own private information. This paper also proposes a new algorithm, called the Graphical RLE (GRLE), which is used to learn the GRE in a dynamic setting. This algorithm is shown to be effective in a variety of scenarios, including games with a large number of players and games with complex information structures.

In this study, we investigate the spread of an epidemic on a dynamic network where individuals can choose to disconnect from their original network and create new connections. We model the epidemic using a stochastic process and analyze its behavior under different conditions. Our findings show that disconnecting from the original network and creating new connections can significantly slow down the spread of the epidemic, even when the new connections are formed randomly. We also explore the impact of different connection probabilities and network sizes on the epidemic's spread. Our results have implications for understanding how social distancing and creating new connections can help prevent the spread of infectious diseases.

The development of particle physics at high-energy colliders relies on precise theoretical predictions, which are encapsulated in parton distribution functions (PDFs). These functions describe the composition of protons and other composite particles in terms of their constituent partons. To ensure the accuracy of experimental measurements, a robust framework is required to fit PDFs to data. This framework must be capable of handling complex calculations, including those for multi-parton interactions, and must be easily accessible to both theoretical physicists and experimentalists. The authors of this work have created a Python-based tool that automates the process of fitting PDFs to data, providing a seamless interface for both groups. This tool is designed to be flexible and extensible, allowing for the inclusion of new observables and processes, and is freely available for use.

Reinforcement learning agents in complex environments often struggle due to limited data, which hinders their ability to learn effectively. To address this issue, researchers have developed methods to reduce the variance of data samples, including the use of replay buffers. However, existing replay buffer techniques are limited in their scope, focusing on specific algorithms and not applicable to a wide range of policy optimization methods. In this paper, we introduce a novel replay buffer technique called Variance Reduction based Experience Replay (VREx), which reduces the variance of data samples by storing and reusing samples from the initial policy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of VREx through extensive experiments on both continuous and discrete control tasks, showing significant improvements in sample efficiency and performance compared to existing methods.

Conversational agents are being developed to handle complex conversations, but current datasets are limited in their ability to capture the breadth of human interactions. To address this, we introduce MultiTalk, a dataset comprising over 10,000 conversations with multiple participants, where each conversation involves at least two turns of conversation between three or more speakers. We also provide a set of guidelines for creating new datasets with branching conversation structures. The data is available in various formats, including a JSON file containing the raw data, a Python package for easy access, and a Jupyter notebook for visualization. The dataset is designed to facilitate the creation of new datasets with branching conversation structures, and we provide a set of guidelines for creating these datasets.

We have developed a fast and efficient method for simulating modified gravity theories, specifically designed for large-scale structure analysis. Our code, built upon the GADGET-2 framework, incorporates a precomputed, time-dependent potential to accelerate the calculation of non-linear gravitational effects. This acceleration technique is applicable to a wide range of modified gravity theories, including DGP, f(R), and other models with similar characteristics. Our simulations demonstrate that our acceleration method yields highly accurate results, closely matching those obtained through direct numerical integration. Our code has been used to generate a set of N-body simulations for the Hu-Sawicki model, covering a range of parameters and cosmological scenarios. These simulations are publicly available for use by the scientific community.

We investigate the relationship between a Gaussian free field and a collection of Schramm-Loewner evolution curves in two-dimensional space. Specifically, we establish that the Gaussian free field can drive the evolution of $N$ independent curves, each following the SLE$_4$ path, under certain conditions. We demonstrate that the curves' evolution can be described using a system of stochastic differential equations driven by a two-dimensional Bessel process of dimension four. Furthermore, we show that the curves' evolution can be characterized using a two-dimensional version of the Schramm-Loewner evolution.

extremely popular, with over 1.5 million websites built on it.  One of its
key features is its wiki-based collaborative editing system, which allows
multiple users to work on the same content simultaneously.  This collaborative
aspect is particularly beneficial for academic and research projects, where
teams of researchers can work together on shared documents.  However, existing
MediaWiki-based solutions for collaborative research lack essential features
such as user authentication, version history, and discussion threads.  To
address this gap, we developed WorkingWiki, a MediaWiki-based platform
specifically designed for collaborative research projects.  WorkingWiki
includes user authentication, version history, discussion threads, and
customizable templates, making it a powerful tool for managing and organizing
research content.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of WorkingWiki through a
case study of a research project, highlighting its benefits and ease of use.

The integration of genome-wide association studies and chromatin interaction maps has been proposed to identify the functional elements associated with complex traits. This study combines data from the ENCODE project and the Roadmap Epigenomics project with 18 human trait GWAS datasets to explore the relationship between chromatin interactions and complex traits. The analysis reveals that the majority of GWAS signals are located in regulatory elements, particularly enhancers, and that these signals are associated with tissue-specific chromatin interactions. The study also identifies specific tissues that are linked to complex traits, such as the pancreas and liver with diabetes, and the brain with psychiatric disorders. Furthermore, the study finds that the majority of GWAS signals are located in open chromatin regions, and that these signals are associated with specific transcription factor binding sites. The study also identifies specific transcription factors that are linked to complex traits, such as FOXA2 and HNF4A with diabetes, and GATA2 and GATA3 with psychiatric disorders. The study's findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between chromatin interactions and complex traits, and may have implications for the development of new therapeutic strategies.

Inertial forces experienced by electrons in a rotating frame can be likened to the Coriolis and centrifugal forces, which are well-known in classical mechanics. This study delves into the consequences of these inertial forces on the interaction between electrons and phonons in a rotating system. It is found that the interaction between electrons and phonons is significantly influenced by the rotation, with the inertial effects becoming more pronounced at higher rotation speeds. The study also reveals that the interaction between electrons and phonons can be either enhanced or suppressed, depending on the direction of rotation. Furthermore, the study finds that the interaction between electrons and phonons can be used to control the direction of rotation, with potential applications in the development of new types of quantum devices.

In dialogue systems, maintaining a diverse range of responses is crucial for engaging and informative conversations. However, current diversity metrics often rely on superficial features like word choice, which can be misleading. This paper proposes a new approach to measuring semantic diversity in conversations using Natural Language Inference (NLI) models. By leveraging these models, we can assess the underlying meaning of responses and ensure a more genuine diversity in conversations. We conducted experiments on various dialogue datasets and found that our NLI-based diversity metric effectively captures the semantic diversity of responses. Furthermore, we developed a new task called Multi-turn Response Generation (MRRG) to evaluate a model's ability to generate diverse responses over multiple turns. Our results demonstrate that incorporating NLI-based diversity in training can lead to more diverse and engaging conversations.

A numerical modeling approach was developed to investigate the impact of rotation on brown dwarfs and giant planets, considering their internal composition and rotation rates. The model incorporates a two-layer structure with a conductive envelope and an adiabatic interior, and was used to calculate the radius, moment of inertia, and rotation period of these objects. The results show that rotation can significantly increase the radius of these objects, with the effect being more pronounced in objects with larger envelopes. The model also reveals that the moment of inertia increases with rotation rate, and that the radius and moment of inertia can be used to estimate the envelope fraction of these objects. The model was also applied to the object GJ 504b, which has a very short rotation period, and found that the object's radius and moment of inertia are consistent with a large envelope fraction. The model was also used to estimate the maximum rotation rate of these objects, and found that the limit depends on the envelope fraction and the rotation axis. The model provides a useful tool for interpreting observations of rotating brown dwarfs and giant planets, and can be used to estimate their internal composition and envelope fraction.

In amplitude analyses, researchers fit complex data using a vast number of parameters, often representing the outcome of a complicated physical process. A key challenge in these analyses is accounting for the detector's influence on the observed data, which can be particularly difficult in multi-body processes. A common approach involves creating a detailed simulation of the detector, but this can be computationally intensive and time-consuming. A more efficient alternative is to use a parametric model that describes the detector's effects, which can be derived from a smaller set of simulated data. This method is demonstrated in the analysis of the decay process $D^0 \to K^+K^-K^+\pi^-$, where the effects of the detector on the four final-state particles are modeled using a parametric approach. The results obtained from this method are comparable to those from a full simulation, but with a significant reduction in computational resources and time.

A novel, comprehensive model for afterglows in relativistic outflows has been developed, which incorporates the effects of energy loss through synchrotron radiation and pair production. This model accounts for the evolution of the radiation spectrum and the temporal and spectral dependencies of the optical depth, which is crucial for determining the peak flux and luminosity. The model is applied to the afterglows of gamma-ray bursts, and the results are compared with observations. The model predicts that the peak flux and luminosity will evolve in a power-law manner, with the spectral index and electron distribution index playing a significant role in this evolution. The model also predicts that the peak flux and luminosity will be affected by the external density and the total energy of the burst. The model is found to be consistent with observations of gamma-ray bursts, and it provides a framework for understanding the evolution of afterglows in relativistic outflows.

A key challenge in parameterized algorithms is developing efficient solutions for vertex modification problems within specific graph classes. This study focuses on the bipartite vertex splitting problem, where the goal is to minimize the number of vertices that need to be removed from a graph to make it bipartite, given a parameter k. We demonstrate that bipartite vertex splitting can be solved in O*(2^k) time, providing a significant improvement over the previous best-known bound of O*(3.73^k) established by Guo and Rutter in 2014.

This paper presents a novel approach to bipedal locomotion by incorporating
a thruster system, which enables more efficient and stable movement. The
thruster-assisted system allows for a wider range of walking speeds and
surmounting obstacles that would otherwise be impassable. The paper outlines
the mathematical framework for the system's dynamics and control, and
demonstrates its effectiveness through simulations and physical experiments.
The results show that the thruster-assisted system can walk at higher speeds
and overcome obstacles that would be impassable for a conventional bipedal
robot. The paper also highlights the potential applications of this approach
in various fields, including search and rescue, space exploration, and
disaster response.

The concept of a total residue map in a valued field is defined as a function that assigns to each element of the field with a non-zero valuation a unique residue in the residue field, such that the residue of the product of two elements equals the product of their individual residues. This paper provides a comprehensive classification of valued fields that possess a total residue map, building on previous work by various authors.

Throttling is a common issue that arises when high-performance computing systems are pushed to their limits, causing a reduction in CPU frequency and performance. This problem is particularly prevalent in high-performance data centers, where the cooling infrastructure may not be able to handle the heat generated by the servers. In this paper, we introduce HyperDegrade, a novel technique that intentionally lowers CPU frequency to prevent throttling and maintain optimal performance. HyperDegrade uses a machine learning model to predict the optimal CPU frequency that minimizes throttling while maximizing performance. Our evaluation on a high-performance computing cluster shows that HyperDegrade can improve performance by up to 10% compared to traditional cooling methods.

We introduce a novel operation called welded crossing change that can transform a welded unknot into any other welded knot without increasing its welded crossing number. This operation is analogous to the standard crossing change but is limited to a specific type of crossing in the welded knot diagram. As a result, any welded knot can be converted into a welded unknot through a finite number of welded crossing changes. This has significant implications for the welded unknotting number, which is defined as the minimum number of welded crossing changes required to transform a given welded knot into a welded unknot. We provide examples of welded knots with a welded unknotting number of 1 and 2, and also establish a relationship between the welded unknotting number and the welded genus.

We demonstrate that the Fox-Hatcher cycle, a specific 3-chain associated with a closed curve in a surface, is equivalent to three times the Vassiliev invariant of order three for that curve. This relationship holds true in the context of a surface.

This paper addresses the challenge of coordinating multiple robots to optimize a shared objective, where each robot has access to a distinct set of tasks and can only interact with a limited number of peers. Unlike previous research, we assume that the robots' communication network is not fully connected, and we develop a decentralized algorithm that enables the group to collectively identify the optimal assignment of tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical simulations.

As technology advances, the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning is becoming increasingly prevalent in various industries. However, the limited availability of data from individual organizations hinders the development of high-quality models. To overcome this challenge, Federated Learning (FL) was introduced, enabling multiple organizations to collaborate on model training while keeping their data private. Unfortunately, FL's traditional approach of sharing data horizontally limits its effectiveness in scenarios where organizations have different sets of features. To address this limitation, Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) was developed, allowing organizations to collaborate on models while retaining their unique data sets. Despite the benefits of VFL, there is a lack of research on the privacy risks associated with this approach. In this paper, we investigate the privacy risks of VFL and present two novel attacks, including a new attack called the "feature-matching attack." We also demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks through experiments and provide a framework for designing privacy attacks on VFL. Our research highlights the importance of considering privacy risks in VFL and provides a foundation for developing more secure and private VFL systems.

Kernel methods are highly effective in machine learning, yet they can be computationally demanding when applied to large datasets. To address this issue, random feature methods have been developed, which utilize random projections to approximate kernels and enable scalable training. In this paper, we introduce a novel kernel approximation technique called Data Dependent Kernel Approximation (DDKA), which generates a random feature map that is specific to the input data. This feature map is used to construct a positive semi-definite kernel, which is then employed in a Support Vector Machine classifier. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through both theoretical analysis and empirical results, which show that DDKA outperforms existing random feature methods in terms of classification accuracy.

This research focuses on the group embedding of $G$ into the wreath product $S_n \wr H$ in the Cartesian decomposition context. We establish the conditions under which this embedding is feasible and develop an efficient algorithm with a time complexity of $O(n)$ to construct the embedding when possible.
This note proves that a compact, locally conformally flat hypersurface in the n-sphere is uniquely determined as a round sphere if its M\"obius scalar curvature is constant and positive.

This research focuses on optimizing power allocation in wireless networks that use simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). The goal is to maximize the sum rate of data transmission while ensuring that devices receive a minimum amount of power from the network. The problem is complex due to the non-convex nature of the power requirements, which are based on the total received power from all signals. To address this challenge, the study proposes an iterative algorithm that alternates between optimizing data transmission rates and power allocation. The results show that the algorithm converges to a stable solution and achieves a significant increase in the sum rate compared to other methods. The study also considers a scenario where devices can switch between different reception modes and finds that the optimal solution involves allocating a small amount of power to one mode and using the other mode for the majority of data transmission.

We investigate the behavior of percolation in randomly filled Cayley trees, focusing on the characteristics of giant clusters that form when the filling probability exceeds a critical threshold. By utilizing matrix-based calculations, we determine the statistical properties of these clusters and find that their sizes follow an exponential distribution, in contrast to the power-law distribution observed in other types of networks. We also examine the relationship between cluster sizes and their connectivity to the network's root, as well as the impact of introducing a bias towards more connected clusters.
